```{r setup}
library(trainingmodels)
```

This version of the package simulates the Banister impulse-response model
from parameters given by the user. It does not estimate parameters from data.

## Theory

**Fitness and fatigue as exponential filters** (MODELS.md, M-01). Each day
$t$ has one training load $w(t)$, the sum of its sessions. A component with
time constant $\tau$ (in days) accumulates the loads and forgets them
exponentially. The literature uses two discrete forms, and the package
offers both through the argument `same_day_load`:

* **"exclude"** (the default): the load of day $t$ affects performance from
  day $t + 1$, as in the R script of Busso & Chalencon (2023),
  $$
  g(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t-1} w(s)\,e^{-(t-s)/\tau}
  = \left[g(t-1) + w(t-1)\right] e^{-1/\tau}.
  $$
  It corresponds to a performance test done before that day's training.
* **"include"**: the load of day $t$ counts on day $t$ at full weight, as in
  Morton, Fitz-Clarke & Banister (1990, Eqs. 4-5),
  $$
  g(t) = \sum_{s=1}^{t} w(s)\,e^{-(t-s)/\tau} = g(t-1)\,e^{-1/\tau} + w(t).
  $$

The two forms are related by $g_{\mathrm{inc}}(t) = g_{\mathrm{exc}}(t) +
w(t)$. They are not equivalent: the same parameters give different numbers.
The load descriptors of the package, such as `rolling_load()`, default to
"include"; the impulse-response models default to "exclude".

The **half-life** of a component, $\tau \ln 2$, is the number of days it
takes to fall to half. Functions take time constants; printed output shows
the half-life next to each one (`half_life()`, `time_constant()`).

The **initial state** $g(0) = g_0$ is 0 by default and can be set by the
user. Under both conventions it adds $g_0\,e^{-t/\tau}$ to day $t$.

**Two-component model** (MODELS.md, M-02; Morton et al. 1990). Fitness $g$
(time constant $\tau_1$) and fatigue $h$ (time constant $\tau_2$) are two
filters of the same loads, and predicted performance is

$$
p(t) = p_0 + k_1\,g(t) - k_2\,h(t),
$$

with baseline $p_0$ and gains $k_1$, $k_2$. Fatigue usually has the larger
gain and the shorter time constant: training lowers performance at first and
raises it later.

**Fitness-only model** (MODELS.md, M-03; as printed in Marchal et al. 2025).
Without the fatigue component,

$$
p(t) = p_0 + k_1\,g(t).
$$

**Response to a single session** (MODELS.md, M-05). The effect on
performance $u$ days after one unit of load is

$$
L(u) = k_1\,e^{-u/\tau_1} - k_2\,e^{-u/\tau_2}.
$$

When $\tau_1 > \tau_2$ and $k_2 > k_1$ the effect is negative at first, turns
positive after `time_to_recover` days and is largest after `time_to_peak`
days (Clarke & Skiba 2013; Busso & Chalencon 2023, Eqs. 12-13):

$$
\text{time\_to\_recover} = \frac{\tau_1 \tau_2}{\tau_1 - \tau_2}
\ln\frac{k_2}{k_1},
\qquad
\text{time\_to\_peak} = \frac{\tau_1 \tau_2}{\tau_1 - \tau_2}
\ln\frac{k_2\,\tau_1}{k_1\,\tau_2}.
$$

These times do not depend on the timing convention; only the effect on the
day of the session does ($k_1 - k_2$ under "include", 0 under "exclude").
They are `NA` when they do not exist: `time_to_recover` when
$k_2 \le k_1$, `time_to_peak` when $k_2 \tau_1 \le k_1 \tau_2$, and both when
$k_1 = 0$, when $\tau_1 \le \tau_2$ or for the fitness-only model. In Busso
& Chalencon (2023), alternative parameter sets with a similar fit gave
small, although statistically significant, differences in the response to a
session; the authors recommend characterising an athlete by that response
rather than by each parameter taken individually.

## Computation

### Morton's example

Morton et al. (1990, Figs. 3-4) train at a load of 100 every day for 60
days and then stop, with $k_1 = 1$, $k_2 = 2$, $\tau_1 = 45$ and
$\tau_2 = 15$, no baseline and the convention "include".

```{r}
x <- as_daily_load(
  data.frame(date = as.Date("2026-01-01") + 0:119,
             load = c(rep(100, 60), rep(0, 60))),
  date = "date", load = "load"
)
inc <- simulate_banister(x, k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, k2 = 2, tau2 = 15,
                         same_day_load = "include")
inc
```

The values agree with the published ones (MODELS.md, M-02):

```{r}
p <- inc$predicted
data.frame(
  quantity = c("k1 g(60)", "k2 h(60)", "Day of minimum",
               "p(47)", "p(48)", "Day of peak after stopping",
               "Peak after stopping"),
  published = c("3,351", "3,044", "16", "about day 47", "",
                "83", "about 1,353"),
  package = c(inc$fitness[60], 2 * inc$fatigue[60], which.min(p),
              p[47], p[48], 60 + which.max(p[61:120]), max(p[61:120]))
)
```

Performance falls during the first 16 days, returns to baseline between
days 47 and 48, and peaks 23 days after training stops. Under the default
convention "exclude" the curve is shifted: each day misses its own load.

```{r}
exc <- simulate_banister(x, k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, k2 = 2, tau2 = 15)
c(include = inc$predicted[60], exclude = exc$predicted[60])
```

```{r morton-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Predicted performance over 120 days under the two timing conventions. Both fall to a minimum on day 16, rise during training, and peak on day 83, 23 days after training stops on day 60."}
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), las = 1, bty = "n", col.axis = "grey30",
          col.lab = "grey30", fg = "grey60")
plot(seq_along(p), inc$predicted, type = "n",
     ylim = range(inc$predicted, exc$predicted),
     xlab = "Day", ylab = "Predicted performance",
     main = "Morton's example: 60 days of training, then rest",
     font.main = 1, cex.main = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey80")
abline(v = 60, col = "grey80", lty = 3)
lines(seq_along(p), inc$predicted, col = "#2a78d6", lwd = 2)
lines(seq_along(p), exc$predicted, col = "#eb6834", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("include", "exclude"),
       col = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

`constant_training()` gives the same curve in closed form, the asymptote of
performance if training never stops, and the day of poorest performance.
The asymptote depends on the convention; the day of the minimum does not.

```{r}
constant_training(100, k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, k2 = 2, tau2 = 15,
                  same_day_load = "include")
constant_training(100, k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, k2 = 2, tau2 = 15)$asymptote
```

### Response to a single session

With Morton's parameters, one session lowers performance for about 16 days
and raises it most after about 40 days:

```{r}
r <- session_response(k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, k2 = 2, tau2 = 15, days = 100)
r
```

```{r session-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Effect of one unit of load on predicted performance over 100 days. It is negative until day 15.6 and largest on day 40.3."}
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), las = 1, bty = "n", col.axis = "grey30",
          col.lab = "grey30", fg = "grey60")
plot(r$curve$day, r$curve$effect, type = "n",
     ylim = c(min(r$curve$effect), 2 * r$peak_effect),
     xlab = "Days after the session", ylab = "Effect per unit of load",
     main = "Response to one session (convention \"exclude\")",
     font.main = 1, cex.main = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey80")
lines(r$curve$day, r$curve$effect, col = "#2a78d6", lwd = 2)
points(c(r$time_to_recover, r$time_to_peak), c(0, r$peak_effect),
       pch = 21, bg = "#2a78d6", col = "white", cex = 1.4)
text(r$time_to_recover, 0, "time_to_recover", pos = 1, col = "grey20")
text(r$time_to_peak, r$peak_effect, "time_to_peak", pos = 3, col = "grey20")
par(op)
```

The fit of Clarke & Skiba (2013, Fig. 8B) gives times of about 12 and 40
days:

```{r}
session_response(k1 = 0.18258, tau1 = 35.821, k2 = 0.23016, tau2 = 21.340)
```

## Limitations

* Parameters are strongly correlated and several parameter sets fit the
  same data almost equally well (Busso & Chalencon 2023; Vermeire et al.
  2022).
* Estimates from local optimisers depend on the starting values (Vermeire et
  al. 2022).
* Adding the fatigue component improved fit but not prediction in two
  datasets (Marchal et al. 2025).
* With 56 to 104 performance tests per swimmer, the mean $R^2$ of the model
  was 0.29, and the mean absolute percentage error of its predictions was
  2.0% and 2.7% in two validation sets (Busso & Chalencon 2023).
* The positive effect is linear in training load. The model therefore
  cannot represent maladaptation to overtraining, and an optimal training
  load before a taper cannot be searched with it (Busso & Chalencon 2023).
  Optimising the model without constraints gives maximal training followed
  by rest (Ceddia et al. 2025, preprint).
* Training is reduced to one number per day, parameters are constant in
  time, and the initial state is assumed.
* The two timing conventions give different numbers; gains obtained under
  one are not comparable with the other.
* This version only simulates: it does not estimate parameters from data.

## References

models for modeling and predicting training effects on performance of
swimmers. *Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise*, 55(7), 1274-1285.

Ceddia D, Bondell H, Taylor P (2025). Mathematical modelling and
optimisation of athletic performance: tapering and periodisation.
arXiv:2505.20859 (preprint).

Clarke DC, Skiba PF (2013). Rationale and resources for teaching the
mathematical modeling of athletic training and performance. *Advances in
Physiology Education*, 37, 134-152.

Marchal A, Benazieb O, Weldegebriel Y, Méline T, Imbach F (2025).
Statistical flaws of the fitness-fatigue sports performance prediction
model. *Scientific Reports*, 15, 3706.

Morton RH, Fitz-Clarke JR, Banister EW (1990). Modeling human performance
in running. *Journal of Applied Physiology*, 69(3), 1171-1177.

Vermeire K, Ghijs M, Bourgois JG, Boone J (2022). The fitness-fatigue model:
what's in the numbers? *International Journal of Sports Physiology and
Performance*, 17, 810-813.
